Congress appropriated funds for the 'suppression of Indian hostilities', but the costs of the [Creek War of 1836](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creek_War_of_1836 "Creek War of 1836") are included in that. An inquiry in extravagance in naval operations found that the Navy had spent about US$511,000 on the war. The investigation did find questionable expenditures. Among other things, while the Army had bought dugout canoes for $10 to $15 apiece, the Navy spent an average of $226 per canoe. The number of Army, Navy and Marine regulars who served in Florida is given as 10,169. About 30,000 militiamen and volunteers also served in the war.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

By the spring 1841, the paymaster general issued a report that found the U.S. government had issued $2,500,000 in payroll to regular army soldiers and an additional $3,500,000 in payroll to citizen soldiers.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-111)

Sources agree that the U.S. Army officially recorded 1,466 deaths in the Second Seminole War, mostly from disease. The number killed in action is less clear. Mahon reports 328 regular Army killed in action, while Missall reports that Seminoles killed 269 officers and men. Almost half of those deaths occurred in the [Dade Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_Massacre "Dade Massacre"), [Battle of Lake Okeechobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Okeechobee "Battle of Lake Okeechobee") and Harney Massacre. Similarly, Mahon reports 69 deaths for the Navy while Missall reports 41 for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, but adds others may have died after being sent out of Florida as _incurable_. Mahon and the Florida Board of State Institutions agree that 55 volunteer officers and men were killed by the Seminoles, while Missall says the number is unknown. There is no figure for how many militiamen and volunteers died of disease or accident, however.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-ReferenceA-112)

The number of white civilians, Seminoles and Black Seminoles killed is uncertain. A northern newspaper carried a report that more than 80 civilians were killed by Indians in Florida in 1839. Nobody was keeping a cumulative account of the number of Indians and Black Seminoles killed, or the number who died of starvation or other privations caused by the war. The people shipped west did not fare well, either. By the end of 1843, 3,824 Indians (including 800 Black Seminoles) had been shipped from Florida to what became the [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"). They were initially settled on the Creek Reservation, which created tensions. The next year, the Florida people numbered 3,136. As of 1962, their numbers had dropped to 2,343 Seminoles in the Indian Territory and perhaps some 1,500 in Florida.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-ReferenceA-112)

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

Peace had come to Florida for a while. The Natives were mostly staying on the reservation, but there were minor clashes. The Florida authorities continued to press for removal of all Natives from Florida. The Natives tried to limit their contacts with the [American settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_pioneer "American pioneer") as much as possible.

As time went on there were more serious incidents. The government resolved once more to remove all Indians from Florida, and applied increasing pressure on the Seminoles until they struck back, starting the Third Seminole War of 1855–1858.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-113)

The **Second Seminole War**, also known as the **Florida War**, was a conflict from 1835 to 1842 in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") between the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and groups of people collectively known as [Seminoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole "Seminole"), consisting of [Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee "Muscogee") and [Black Seminoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Seminoles "Black Seminoles") as well as other allied tribes (see below). It was part of a series of conflicts called the [Seminole Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole_Wars "Seminole Wars"). The Second Seminole War, often referred to as _the_ Seminole War, is regarded as "the longest and most costly of the [Indian conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Indian_Wars "American Indian Wars") of the United States".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-13) After the [Treaty of Payne's Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Payne's_Landing "Treaty of Payne's Landing") in 1832 that called for the Seminoles' removal from Florida, tensions rose until fierce hostilities occurred in [Dade's massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_battle "Dade battle") in 1835. This engagement officially started the war although there were a series of incidents leading up to the Dade battle. The Seminoles and the U.S. forces engaged in mostly small engagements for more than six years. By 1842, only a few hundred native people remained in Florida. Although no peace treaty was ever signed, the war was declared over on August 14, 1842, by Colonel [William Jenkins Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jenkins_Worth "William Jenkins Worth").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-14)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Bands from various tribes in the [southeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") had moved into the unoccupied lands in Florida in the 18th century. These included [Alabamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_(people) "Alabama (people)"), [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw"), [Yamasees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamasee "Yamasee"), [Yuchis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuchi "Yuchi") and [Muscogees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee "Muscogee") (then called "Creeks"). The Muscogees were the largest group, and included people from the Lower Towns and Upper Towns of the [Muscogee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee#Rise_of_the_Muscogee_Confederacy "Muscogee"), and both [Hitchiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikasuki_language "Mikasuki language") and [Muscogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee_language "Muscogee language") speakers. One group of Hitchiti speakers, the Mikasuki, settled around what is now [Lake Miccosukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Miccosukee "Lake Miccosukee") near [Tallahassee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallahassee,_Florida "Tallahassee, Florida"). Another group of Hitchiti speakers settled around the [Alachua Prairie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paynes_Prairie "Paynes Prairie") in what is now [Alachua County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alachua_County,_Florida "Alachua County, Florida") (see [Ahaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahaya "Ahaya")). The Spanish in [St. Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Augustine,_Florida "St. Augustine, Florida") began calling the Alachua Muscogees _cimarrones_, which roughly meant "wild ones" or "runaways",[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-16) and which is the probable origin of "Seminole". This name was eventually also applied to the other groups in Florida, although the Native Americans still regarded themselves as members of different tribes. Other groups in Florida at the time of the Seminole Wars included "[Spanish Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Indians "Spanish Indians")", so called because it was believed that they were descended from [Calusas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calusa "Calusa"), and "rancho Indians", persons of Native American ancestry, possibly both Calusa and Muscogee, and mixed Native American/Spanish ancestry, living at Spanish/Cuban [fishing ranchos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_ranchos "Fishing ranchos") on the Florida coast.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-17) For a brief period after the start of the war, these rancho Indians, particularly those residing along Tampa Bay, were offered protection. However, they were also eventually forced onto reservations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuker199711-18)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Moultriecreekreservation.PNG/250px-Moultriecreekreservation.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moultriecreekreservation.PNG)

The Treaty of Moultrie Creek provided for a reservation in central Florida for the Seminoles.

The United States and Spain were at odds over Florida after the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)") ended the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") and returned [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Florida "East Florida") and [West Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Florida "West Florida") to Spanish control. The United States disputed the boundaries of West Florida. They accused the Spanish authorities of harboring fugitive slaves (see the [Negro Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negro_Fort "Negro Fort")) and of failing to restrain the Native Americans living in Florida from raiding the United States. Starting in 1810, the United States occupied and annexed parts of [West Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_West_Florida "Republic of West Florida"). Also, the [Patriot War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_War_(Florida) "Patriot War (Florida)") of 1812 was part of these ongoing conflicts. In 1818, [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") led an invasion of [Spanish Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Florida "Spanish Florida"), during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") and the [Creek War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creek_War "Creek War") leading to the [First Seminole War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Seminole_War "First Seminole War").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-19)

The United States acquired Florida from Spain through the [Adams–Onís Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams%E2%80%93On%C3%ADs_Treaty "Adams–Onís Treaty") in 1819 and took possession of the territory in 1821. Now that Florida belonged to the United States, settlers pressured the government to remove the Seminole and their allies altogether. In 1823 the government negotiated the [Treaty of Moultrie Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Moultrie_Creek "Treaty of Moultrie Creek") with the Seminoles, establishing a reservation for them in the middle of the territory. Six chiefs, however, were allowed to keep their villages along the [Apalachicola River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apalachicola_River "Apalachicola River") (see [Neamathla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neamathla "Neamathla")).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-20)

### Move to the reservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Move to the reservation")]

The Seminoles gave up their lands in the panhandle and slowly settled into the reservation, although they occasionally had clashes with European Americans. Colonel (later General) [Duncan Lamont Clinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Lamont_Clinch "Duncan Lamont Clinch") was placed in charge of the Army units in Florida. [Fort King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_King "Fort King") was built near the reservation agency, at the site of present-day [Ocala, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocala,_Florida "Ocala, Florida").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-21)

By early 1827, the Army reported that the Seminoles were on the reservation and Florida was peaceful. This peace lasted for five years, during which time there were repeated calls for the Seminoles to be sent west of the Mississippi. The Seminoles were opposed to the move, and especially to the suggestion that they should be placed on the Creek reservation. Most European Americans regarded the Seminoles as simply Creeks who had recently moved to Florida, while the Seminoles claimed Florida as their home and denied that they had any connection with the Creeks.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-22)

The status of runaway slaves was a continuing irritation between Seminoles and European Americans. "The major problem was not with them [Seminoles] but with the Indian-[Negros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negros "Negros")."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Mahon251-23) General Taylor would not, being a _slave holder_ himself, deny "the Seminoles of their Negros", and "in practice", handed his captives over to Lt. J. G. Reynolds, [U.S. Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Marine_Corps "U.S. Marine Corps"), "in charge of immigration."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Mahon251-23) Spain had given freedom to slaves who escaped to Florida under their rule, although the U.S. did not recognize it. Over the years, those who became known as [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Seminoles "Black Seminoles") or Negro [Seminoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminoles "Seminoles") established communities separate from the Seminole villages, and the two peoples had close alliances although they maintained separate cultures. "Negroes among the Seminoles constituted a threat to the [institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institution "Institution") of [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") north of the Spanish border.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Mahon20-24) Slave holders in Mississippi and other border areas were aware of this and "constantly accused the Indians of stealing their _Negroes._ However, this "accusation" was often reversed; whites were raiding Florida and forcibly stealing the red men's slaves.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Mahon20-24)

Worried about the possibility of an Indian uprising and/or an armed slave rebellion, Governor DuVal requested additional Federal troops for Florida. Instead, Fort King was closed in 1828. The Seminoles, short of food and finding the hunting becoming poorer on the reservation, were wandering off of it more often. Also in 1828, Andrew Jackson, the old enemy of the Seminoles, was elected [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"). In 1830 Congress passed the [Indian Removal Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act "Indian Removal Act"). They wanted to solve the problems with the Seminoles by moving them to west of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-25)

### Treaty of Payne's Landing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Treaty of Payne's Landing")]

Main article: [Treaty of Payne's Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Payne's_Landing "Treaty of Payne's Landing")

In the spring of 1832, the Seminoles on the reservation were called to a meeting at Payne's Landing on the [Oklawaha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklawaha_River "Oklawaha River"). The treaty negotiated there called for the Seminoles to move west, if the land was found to be suitable. They were to be settled on the Creek reservation and become part of the Creek tribe. The delegation of seven chiefs who were to inspect the new reservation did not leave Florida until October 1832. After the chiefs had toured the area for several months and had conferred with the Creeks who had already been settled there, on March 28, 1833, the federal government produced a treaty with the chiefs' signatures.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Missall_83-85-26)

Upon their return to Florida, however, most of the chiefs renounced the statement, claiming that they had not signed it, or that they had been forced to sign it. They said they did not have the power to decide for all the tribes and bands that resided on the reservation. Even some U.S. Army officers claimed that the chiefs had been "wheedled and bullied into signing." Others noted "there is evidence of trickery by the whites in the way the treaty is phrased."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-27) The members of the villages in the area of the Apalachicola River were more easily persuaded, however, as they suffered more encroachment from European Americans; they went west in 1834.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Missall_83-85-26)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/An_Indian_Town%2C_Residence_of_a_Chief.jpg/250px-An_Indian_Town%2C_Residence_of_a_Chief.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:An_Indian_Town,_Residence_of_a_Chief.jpg)

This view of a Seminole village shows the log cabins they lived in prior to the disruptions of the Second Seminole War.

The [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") finally ratified the [Treaty of Payne's Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Payne's_Landing "Treaty of Payne's Landing") in April 1834. The treaty had given the Seminoles three years to move west of the Mississippi. The government interpreted the three years as starting 1832, and expected the Seminoles to move in 1835. Fort King was reopened in 1834. A new Seminole agent, Wiley Thompson, had been appointed in 1834, and the task of persuading the Seminoles to move fell to him. He called the chiefs together at Fort King in October 1834 to talk to them about the removal to the west. The Seminoles informed Thompson that they had no intention of moving, and that they did not feel bound by the Treaty of Payne's Landing. Thompson requested reinforcements for [Fort King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_King "Fort King") and [Fort Brooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Brooke "Fort Brooke"), reporting that, "the Indians after they had received the Annuity, purchased an unusually large quantity of Powder & Lead." General Clinch also warned Washington that the Seminoles did not intend to move, and that more troops would be needed to force them to move. In March 1835 Thompson called the chiefs together to read a letter from President Andrew Jackson to them. In his letter, Jackson said, "Should you... refuse to move, I have then directed the Commanding officer to remove you by force." The chiefs asked for thirty days to respond. A month later the Seminole chiefs told Thompson that they would not move west. Thompson and the chiefs began arguing, and General Clinch had to intervene to prevent bloodshed. Eventually, eight of the chiefs agreed to move west, but asked to delay the move until the end of the year, and Thompson and Clinch agreed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-28)

Five of the most important Seminole chiefs, including [Micanopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micanopy "Micanopy") of the Alachua Seminoles, had not agreed to the move. In retaliation, Thompson declared that those chiefs were removed from their positions. As relations with the Seminoles deteriorated, Thompson forbade the sale of guns and ammunition to them. [Osceola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osceola "Osceola"), a young warrior beginning to be noticed by the European Americans, was particularly upset by the ban, feeling that it equated Seminoles with slaves and said, "The white man shall not make me black. I will make the white man red with blood; and then blacken him in the sun and rain ... and the buzzard live upon his flesh." In spite of this, Thompson considered Osceola to be a friend, and gave him a rifle. Later, though, when Osceola was causing trouble, Thompson had him locked up at Fort King for a night. The next day, in order to secure his release, Osceola agreed to abide by the Treaty of Payne's Landing and to bring his followers in.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-29)

The situation grew worse. A group of European Americans assaulted some Indians sitting around a campfire. Two more Indians came up during the assault and opened fire on the European Americans. Three European Americans were wounded, and one Indian was killed and one wounded. In August 1835, Private Kinsley Dalton (for whom [Dalton, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton,_Georgia "Dalton, Georgia"), is named) was killed by Seminoles as he was carrying the mail from Fort Brooke to Fort King. In November, Chief Charley Emathla, wanting no part of a war, led his people to Fort Brooke, where they were to board ships to go west. This was considered a betrayal by other Seminoles. Osceola met Charley Emathla on the trail to Fort King and killed him.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-30)

## The Dade Battle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Dade Battle")]

Main article: [Dade Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_Battle "Dade Battle")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Florida_massacre_1836.jpeg/250px-Florida_massacre_1836.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Florida_massacre_1836.jpeg)

Fictional massacres depicted in _An Authentic Narrative of the Seminole War._[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-:0-31)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Seminolesmassacreingwhites.jpg/250px-Seminolesmassacreingwhites.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seminolesmassacreingwhites.jpg)

Fictional massacres depicted in _An Authentic Narrative of the Seminole War._[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-:0-31)

As the realization that the Seminoles would resist relocation sank in, Florida began preparing for war. The St. Augustine Militia asked the [War Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_War "United States Department of War") for the loan of 500 muskets. Five hundred volunteers were mobilized under Brig. Gen. [Richard K. Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_K._Call "Richard K. Call"). Indian war parties raided farms and settlements, and families fled to forts, large towns, or out of the territory altogether. A war party led by Osceola captured a Florida militia supply train, killing eight of its guards and wounding six others. Most of the goods taken were recovered by the militia in another fight a few days later. Sugar plantations along the Atlantic coast south of St. Augustine were destroyed, with many of the slaves on the plantations joining the Seminoles.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-32)

The U.S. Army had 11 companies, about 550 soldiers, stationed in Florida. [Fort King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_King "Fort King") had only one company of soldiers, and it was feared that they might be overrun by the Seminoles. There were three companies at Fort Brooke, with another two expected on the way, so it was decided to send two companies to Fort King. On December 23, 1835, the two companies, totaling 110 men, left [Fort Brooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Brooke "Fort Brooke") under the command of Maj. [Francis L. Dade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_L._Dade "Francis L. Dade"). Seminoles shadowed the marching soldiers for five days. On December 28 the Seminoles ambushed the soldiers, and killed all but three of the command, which became known as the [Dade Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade_Massacre "Dade Massacre"). Only three white men survived the battle. Pvt Edwin DeCourcey was hunted down and killed by a Seminole the next day. The other two survivors, Pvt Ransom Clarke and Pvt Joseph Sprague, returned to Fort Brooke. Only Clarke, who ultimately succumbed to his wounds 5 years later, dying on November 18, 1840, at the age of 28, left any account of the battle from the Army's perspective. Entitled _"The Surprising Adventures of Ransom Clark, Among the Indians in Florida"_, it was published in 1839 by J. Orlando Orton and "printed by Johnson and Marble in [Binghamton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binghamton,_New_York "Binghamton, New York")."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-33)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-34) Joseph Sprague suffered a "[shattered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_fracture "Bone fracture")[arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm "Arm")",[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Laumer266-35) served in the army until March 1843, and lived out his days near [White Springs, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Springs,_Florida "White Springs, Florida"), until possibly 1848. No written material from Sprague's personal military [experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience "Experience")'s has ever surfaced.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-Laumer266-35) The Seminoles lost three men killed, with five wounded. On the same day as the Dade Massacre, Osceola and his followers shot and killed [Wiley Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley_Thompson "Wiley Thompson") and six others outside of Fort King.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-36)

In February, Major [Ethan Allen Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethan_A._Hitchcock_(general) "Ethan A. Hitchcock (general)") was among those who found the remains of the Dade party. In his journal he wrote about the discovery and vented his bitter discontent with the conflict:

> The government is in the wrong, and this is the chief cause of the persevering opposition of the Indians, who have nobly defended their country against our attempt to enforce a fraudulent treaty. The natives used every means to avoid a war, but were forced into it by the tyranny of our government.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-37)

On December 29, General Clinch left Fort Drane (recently established on Clinch's plantation, about twenty miles (32 km) northwest of Fort King) with 750 soldiers, including 500 volunteers on an enlistment due to end January 1, 1836. They were going to a Seminole stronghold called the [Cove of the Withlacoochee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cove_of_the_Withlacoochee "Cove of the Withlacoochee"), an area of many lakes on the southwest side of the [Withlacoochee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withlacoochee_River_(Florida) "Withlacoochee River (Florida)"). When they reached the river, they could not find the ford, and Clinch had his regular troops ferried across the river in a single canoe they had found. Once they were across and had relaxed, the Seminoles attacked. The troops survived only by fixing bayonets and charging the Seminoles, at the cost of four dead and 59 wounded. The militia provided cover as the Army troops withdrew across the river.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-38)

On January 6, 1836, a band of Seminoles attacked the [coontie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coontie "Coontie") plantation of [William Cooley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cooley "William Cooley") on the [New River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_River_(Broward_County,_Florida) "New River (Broward County, Florida)") (in present-day [Fort Lauderdale, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida "Fort Lauderdale, Florida")), killing his wife and children and the children's tutor. The other residents of the New River area and of the [Biscayne Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscayne_Bay "Biscayne Bay") country to the south fled to Key West.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-39) On January 17, volunteers and Seminoles met south of St. Augustine at the [Battle of Dunlawton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunlawton_Plantation_and_Sugar_Mill "Dunlawton Plantation and Sugar Mill"). The volunteers lost four men, with thirteen wounded.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-40) On January 19, 1836, the Navy [sloop-of-war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloop-of-war "Sloop-of-war")[_Vandalia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Vandalia_(1828) "USS Vandalia (1828)") was dispatched to Tampa Bay from Pensacola. On the same day 57 [U.S. Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") were dispatched from Key West to help man Fort Brooke.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-41)

## General Gaines' expedition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: General Gaines' expedition")]

The regular American army was very small at the time, with fewer than 7,500 men manning a total of 53 posts.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-42) It was spread thin, with the Canada–U.S. border to guard, coastal fortifications to man, and especially, Indians to move west and then watch and keep separated from white settlers. Temporary needs for additional troops were filled by state and territory militias, and by self-organized volunteer units. As news and rumors of the fighting spread, action was taken on many levels. Maj. Gen. [Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott") was placed in charge of the war. Congress appropriated US$620,000 for the war. Volunteer companies began forming in Alabama, Georgia and [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"). General [Edmund P. Gaines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_P._Gaines "Edmund P. Gaines") put together a force of 1,100 regulars and volunteers in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") and sailed with them to Fort Brooke.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-43) A lack of arms was also an issue, with only two arsenals located in Florida, one at Fort Brooke and the other at Fort Marion, with a third under construction in what is now [Chattahoochee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattahoochee,_Florida "Chattahoochee, Florida").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-44)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Dademassacresite.jpg/250px-Dademassacresite.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dademassacresite.jpg)

_Viewing the demise of Major Dade and his Command_

When Gaines reached Fort Brooke, he found it low on supplies. Believing that General Scott had sent supplies to Fort King, Gaines led his men on to Fort King. Along the road they found the site of the Dade Massacre, and buried the bodies in three mass graves. The force reached Fort King after nine days, only to find it was very short on supplies. After receiving seven days' worth of rations from General Clinch at Fort Drane, Gaines headed back for Fort Brooke. Hoping to accomplish something for his efforts, Gaines took his men on a different route back to Fort Brooke, intending to engage the Seminoles in their stronghold in the Cove of the Withlacoochee River. Due to a lack of knowledge of the country, the Gaines party reached the same point on the Withlacoochee where Clinch had met the Seminoles one-and-a-half months earlier, and it took another day to find the ford while the two sides exchanged gunfire across the river.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-45)

When a crossing was attempted at the ford of the Withlacoochee, Lt. James Izard was wounded (and later died), and General Gaines was stuck by a bullet. Unable to ford the river, and not having enough ration to return to Fort King, Gaines and his men constructed a fortification, called Camp Izard, and sent word to General Clinch. Gaines hoped that the Seminoles would concentrate around Camp Izard, and that Clinch's forces could then hit the Seminoles in their flank, crushing them between the two forces. General Scott, however, who was in charge of the war, ordered Clinch to stay at Fort Drane. Gaines's men were soon reduced to eating their horses and mules, and an occasional dog, while a battle went on for eight days. Still at Fort Drane, Clinch requested that General Scott change his orders and allow him to go to Gaines' aid. Clinch finally decided to disobey Scott and left to join Gaines just one day before Scott's permission to do so arrived at Fort Drane. Clinch and his men reached Camp Izard on March 6, chasing away the Seminoles.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-46)

## General Scott's campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: General Scott's campaign")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Pilaklikaha.png/250px-Pilaklikaha.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pilaklikaha.png)

Gen. Eustis burned Pilaklikaha, or Abraham's Town, on his way to join Gen. Scott's campaign.

General Scott had begun assembling men and supplies for a grand campaign against the Seminoles. Three columns, totaling 5,000 men, were to converge on the Cove of the Withlacoochee, trapping the Seminoles with a force large enough to defeat them. Scott would accompany one column, under the command of General Clinch, moving south from [Fort Drane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Drane "Fort Drane"). A second column, under Brig. Gen. [Abraham Eustis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Eustis "Abraham Eustis"), would travel southwest from Volusia, a town on the [St. Johns River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Johns_River "St. Johns River"). The third wing, under the command of Col. William Lindsay, would move north from [Fort Brooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Brooke "Fort Brooke"). The plan was for the three columns to arrive at the Cove simultaneously so as to prevent the Seminoles from escaping. Eustis and Lindsay were supposed to be in place on March 25, so that Clinch's column could drive the Seminoles into them.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-47)

On the way from St. Augustine to Volusia to take up his starting position, Gen. Eustis found Pilaklikaha, or Palatlakaha ([Palatka, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatka,_Florida "Palatka, Florida")), also known as Abraham's Town. Abraham had been a member of the [Corps of Colonial Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corps_of_Colonial_Marines "Corps of Colonial Marines") and was present at, and taken into custody, at the [Battle of Negro Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Negro_Fort "Battle of Negro Fort"). In custody only a short time, he was a Black Seminole leader, and interpreter for the Seminoles, who played a critical role during the Second Seminole War.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-48):51 Eustis burned the town before moving on to Volusia.

All three columns were delayed. Eustis was two days late departing Volusia because of an attack by the Seminoles. Clinch's and Lindsay's columns only reached their positions on March 28. Because of problems crossing through uncharted territory, Eustis's column did not arrive until March 30. Clinch crossed the Withlacoochee on March 29 to attack the Seminoles in the Cove, but found the villages deserted. Eustis's column did fight a skirmish with some Seminoles before reaching its assigned position, but the whole action had killed or captured only a few Seminoles. On March 31 all three commanders, running low on supplies, headed for Fort Brooke. The failure of the expedition to effectively engage the Seminoles was seen as a defeat, and was blamed on insufficient time for planning and an inhospitable climate.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-49)

## The Army retreats, Governor Call tries his hand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Army retreats, Governor Call tries his hand")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Attackblockhouse.png/250px-Attackblockhouse.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attackblockhouse.png)

_Attack of the Seminoles on the blockhouse_

April 1836 did not go well for the Army. Seminoles attacked a number of forts, including Camp Cooper in the Cove, Fort Alabama on the [Hillsborough River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsborough_River_(Florida) "Hillsborough River (Florida)") north of Fort Brooke, Fort Barnwell near [Volusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volusia,_Florida "Volusia, Florida"), and Fort Drane itself. The Seminoles also burned the sugar works on Clinch's plantation. After that, Clinch resigned his commission and left the territory. Fort Alabama was abandoned in late April. In late May, Fort King was also abandoned. In June the soldiers in a blockhouse on the Withlacoochee were rescued after being besieged by the Seminoles for 48 days. On July 23, 1836, Seminoles attacked the [Cape Florida lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Florida_Light#Attack_on_the_lighthouse "Cape Florida Light"), severely wounding the assistant keeper in charge, killing his assistant, and burning the lighthouse. The lighthouse was not repaired until 1846. Fort Drane and Fort Defiance successfully drove Seminoles away in early June, each using a single artillery piece in support of troops charging Seminoles.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-50)

The Army was suffering terribly from illness; at the time summer in Florida was called the "sickly season". On July 14, Fort Drane was abandoned because of illness, with five out of seven officers and 140 men on the sick list. Troops and supplies from the abandoned fort were sent to Fort Defiance, less than 10 miles (16 km) away. Seminoles attacked the convoy before it could reach Fort Defiance, and the convoy was only able to reach its goal after troops from Fort Defiance arrived to support them. By the end of August, Fort Defiance, on the edge of the Alachua Prairie, was also abandoned. Seeing that the war promised to be long and expensive, Congress appropriated another US$1.5 million, and allowed volunteers to enlist for up to a year.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-52)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Second_Seminole_War_Broadside%2C_1836.jpg/250px-Second_Seminole_War_Broadside%2C_1836.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Seminole_War_Broadside,_1836.jpg)

1836 [broadside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadside_(naval) "Broadside (naval)")

[Richard Keith Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_K._Call "Richard K. Call"), who had led the Florida volunteers as a Brig. Gen. when Clinch marched on the Cove of the Withlacoochee in December 1835, had been appointed Governor of the Territory of Florida on March 16, 1836. Governor Call proposed a summer campaign using militia and volunteers instead of regular Army troops. The War Department agreed to this proposal, but delays in preparations meant the campaign did not start until the end of September. Call also intended to attack the Cove of the Withlacoochee. He sent most of his supplies down the west coast of the peninsula and up the Withlacoochee to set up a supply base. With the main body of his men he marched to the now abandoned Fort Drane, and then on to the Withlacoochee, which they reached on October 13. The Withlacoochee was flooding and could not be forded. The army could not make rafts for a crossing because they had not brought any axes with them. In addition, Seminoles on the other side of the river were shooting at any soldier who showed himself along the river. Call then turned west along the north bank of the river to reach the supply depot. However, the steamer bringing the supplies had sunk in the lower part of the river, and the supply depot was far downstream from where Call was expecting it. Out of food, Call led his men back to Fort Drane, another failed expedition against the Cove.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-53)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Fortbarnwell.png/250px-Fortbarnwell.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fortbarnwell.png)

_Camp Volusia or Fort Barnwell on the Saint Johns River_

In mid-November Call tried again. His forces made it across the Withlacoochee this time, but found the Cove abandoned. Call divided his forces, and proceeded south along the river. On November 17, Seminoles were routed from a large camp. There was another battle the next day, and the Seminoles were assumed to be headed for the Wahoo Swamp. Call waited to bring the other column across the river, then entered the Wahoo Swamp on November 21. The Seminoles resisted the advance in the [Battle of Wahoo Swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wahoo_Swamp "Battle of Wahoo Swamp"), as their families were close by, but had to retreat across a stream. Major David Moniac, who was part Creek and possibly the first Native American to graduate from [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy"), tried to determine how deep the stream was, but was shot and killed by the Seminoles.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-54)

Faced with trying to cross a stream of unknown depth under hostile fire, and with supplies again running short, Call withdrew and led his men to Volusia. On December 9, Call was relieved of command and replaced by Maj. Gen. [Thomas Jesup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jesup "Thomas Jesup"), who took the troops back to Fort Brooke. The enlistments of the volunteers were up at the end of December and they went home.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-55)

## Jesup takes command

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Jesup takes command")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Florida_war_1837_-_en.svg/250px-Florida_war_1837_-_en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Florida_war_1837_-_en.svg)

Jesup campaign

In 1836, the U.S. Army had just four Major Generals. [Alexander Macomb, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Macomb,_Jr. "Alexander Macomb, Jr.") was the commanding general of the Army. Edmund Gaines and Winfield Scott had each taken to the field and failed to defeat the Seminoles. [Thomas Jesup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jesup "Thomas Jesup") was the last Major General available. Jesup had just suppressed an uprising by the Creeks of western Georgia and eastern Alabama (the [Creek War of 1836](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creek_War_of_1836 "Creek War of 1836")), upstaging Winfield Scott in the process. Jesup brought a new approach to the war. Instead of sending large columns out to try to force the Seminoles into a set-piece battle, he concentrated on wearing the Seminoles down. This required a large military presence in Florida, and Jesup eventually had a force of more than 9,000 men under his command. About half of the force were volunteers and militia; he also brought a regiment of friendly [Creeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee "Muscogee") from Alabama who had been involved in the Second Creek War.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-56) The force also included a brigade of Marines, and Navy and [United States Revenue Cutter Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Revenue_Cutter_Service "United States Revenue Cutter Service") (AKA: Revenue Marine) personnel patrolling the coast and inland rivers and streams. In all the Revenue Marine committed 8 Cutters to operations in Florida during the war.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-57)

The U.S. Navy and the Revenue Marine both worked with the Army from the beginning of the war. Navy ships and revenue cutters ferried men and supplies to Army posts. They patrolled the Florida coast to gather information on and intercept Seminoles, and to block smuggling of arms and supplies to the Seminoles. Sailors and Marines helped man Army forts that were short of manpower. Sailors, Marines, and the Cuttermen of the Revenue Marine participated in expeditions into the interior of Florida, both by boat and on land. Against those numbers the Seminoles had started the war with between 900 and 1,400 warriors, and with no means of replacing their losses.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-58) The total population of the Seminoles in 1836 was estimated at 6,000 up to 10,000 people.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-59)

## Truce and reversal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Truce and reversal")]

January 1837 saw a change in the war. In various actions a number of Seminoles and Black Seminoles were killed or captured. At the _Battle of Hatchee-Lustee_, the Marine brigade, "succeeded in capturing the horses and baggage of the enemy, with twenty-five Indians and [negroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negroes "Negroes"), principally women and children."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-60) At the end of January some Seminole chiefs sent messengers to Jesup, and a truce was arranged. Fighting did not stop right away, and a meeting between Jesup and the chiefs did not occur until near the end of February. In March a 'Capitulation' was signed by a number of chiefs, including Micanopy, stipulating that the Seminoles could be accompanied by their allies and "their negroes, their 'bona fide' property" in their relocation to the West.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-61)

Even as Seminoles began to come into the Army camps to await transportation west, slave catchers were claiming blacks living with the Seminoles. As the Seminoles had no written records of ownership, they generally lost in disputes over ownership. Other whites were trying to have Seminoles arrested for alleged crimes or debts. All of this made the Seminoles suspicious of promises made by Jesup. On the other hand, it was noted that many of the warriors coming into the transportation camps had not brought their families, and seemed mainly to be interested in collecting supplies. By the end of May, many chiefs, including Micanopy, had surrendered. Two important leaders, Osceola and [Ar-pi-uck-i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ar-pi-uck-i "Ar-pi-uck-i") (Sam Jones), had not surrendered, however, and were known to be vehemently opposed to relocation. On June 2 these two leaders with about 200 followers entered the poorly guarded holding camp at Fort Brooke and led away the 700 Seminoles there who had surrendered.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-62)

The war did not immediately resume on a large scale. General Jesup had thought that the surrender of so many Seminoles meant the war was ending, and had not planned a long campaign. Many of the soldiers had been assigned elsewhere, or, in the case of militias and volunteers, released from duty. It was also getting into summer, the 'sickly season', and the Army did not fight aggressively in Florida during the summer. The [Panic of 1837](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1837 "Panic of 1837") was reducing government revenues, but Congress appropriated another US$1.6 million for the war. In August the Army stopped supplying rations to civilians who had taken refuge at its forts.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-63)

## Captures and false flags

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Captures and false flags")]

Jesup kept pressure on the Seminoles by sending small units into the field. Many of the blacks with the Seminoles began turning themselves in. After a couple of swings in policy on dealing with fugitive slaves, Jesup ended up sending most of them west to join the Seminoles that were already in Indian territory. On September 10, 1837, the Army and militias captured a band of Mikasukis including King Phillip, one of the most important chiefs in Florida. The next night the same command captured a band of Yuchis, including their leader, [Uchee Billy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uchee_Billy "Uchee Billy").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-64)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Osceolaseized.jpg/250px-Osceolaseized.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Osceolaseized.jpg)

Osceola was seized at the orders of Gen. Jesup when he appeared for a meeting under a white flag.

General Jesup had King Phillip send a message to his son [Coacoochee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Cat_(Seminole) "Wild Cat (Seminole)") (Wild Cat) to arrange a meeting with Jesup. When Coacoochee arrived under a flag of truce, Jesup arrested him. In October Osceola and Coa Hadjo, another chief, requested a parley with Jesup. A meeting was arranged south of St. Augustine. When Osceola and Coa Hadjo arrived for the meeting, also under a white flag, they were arrested. Osceola was dead within three months of his capture, in prison at [Fort Moultrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Moultrie_National_Monument "Fort Moultrie National Monument") in [Charleston, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina"). Not all of the Seminoles captured by the Army stayed captured. While Osceola was still held at [Fort Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Marion "Fort Marion") (Castillo de San Marcos) in St. Augustine, twenty Seminoles held in the same cell with him and King Phillip escaped through a narrow window. The escapees included Coacoochee and [John Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Horse "John Horse"), a Black Seminole leader.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-65) "Undoubtedly the general violated the rules of civilized warfare...[and] he was still writing justifications of it twenty-one years later" for an act that "hardly seems worthwhile to try to grace the capture with any other label than [treachery](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/treachery "wiktionary:treachery")."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-66)

A delegation of [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee") was sent to Florida to try to talk the Seminoles into moving west. When Micanopy and others came in to meet the Cherokees, General Jesup had the Seminoles held. [John Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ross_(Cherokee_chief) "John Ross (Cherokee chief)"), the head of the Cherokee delegation, protested, but to no avail. Jesup replied that he had told the Cherokees that no Seminole who came in would be allowed to return home.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-67)

## Zachary Taylor and the Battle of Lake Okeechobee

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Zachary Taylor and the Battle of Lake Okeechobee")]

Main article: [Battle of Lake Okeechobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Okeechobee "Battle of Lake Okeechobee")

Jesup now had a large army assembled, including volunteers from as far away as [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania")—so many men, in fact, that he had trouble feeding all of them. Jesup's plan was to sweep down the peninsula with multiple columns, pushing the Seminoles further south. General [Joseph Marion Hernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Marion_Hern%C3%A1ndez "Joseph Marion Hernández") led a column down the east coast. General Eustis took his column up the St. Johns River (southward). Colonel [Zachary Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor "Zachary Taylor") led a column from Fort Brooke into the middle of the state, and then southward between the [Kissimmee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kissimmee_River "Kissimmee River") and the [Peace River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_River_(Florida) "Peace River (Florida)"). Other commands cleared out the areas between the St. Johns and the Oklawaha River, between the Oklawaha and the Withlacoochee River, and along the [Caloosahatchee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caloosahatchee_River "Caloosahatchee River"). A joint Army-Navy unit patrolled the lower east coast of Florida. Other troops patrolled the northern part of the territory to protect against Seminole raids.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-68)

Colonel Taylor saw the first major action of the campaign. Leaving Fort Gardiner on the upper Kissimmee with 1,000 men on December 19, Taylor headed towards [Lake Okeechobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Okeechobee "Lake Okeechobee"). In the first two days out ninety Seminoles surrendered. On the third day Taylor stopped to build [Fort Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Basinger,_Florida "Fort Basinger, Florida"), where he left his sick and enough men to guard the Seminoles that had surrendered. Three days later, on Christmas Day, 1837, Taylor's column caught up with the main body of the Seminoles on the north shore of Lake Okeechobee.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-69)

The Seminoles led by [Halpatter Tustenuggee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halpatter_Tustenuggee "Halpatter Tustenuggee") (Alligator]), [Ar-pi-uck-i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ar-pi-uck-i "Ar-pi-uck-i") (Sam Jones), and the recently escaped Coacoochee, were well positioned in a [hammock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammock_(ecology) "Hammock (ecology)") surrounded by [sawgrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cladium "Cladium"). The ground was thick mud, and sawgrass easily cuts and burns the skin. Taylor had about 800 men, while the Seminoles numbered less than 400. Taylor sent the Missouri volunteers in first. Colonel [Richard Gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gentry_(Missouri_politician) "Richard Gentry (Missouri politician)"), three other officers and more than twenty enlisted men were killed before the volunteers retreated. Next in were 200 soldiers of the [6th Infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._6th_Infantry_Regiment "U.S. 6th Infantry Regiment"), who lost four officers and suffered nearly 40% casualties before they withdrew. Then it was the turn of the 4th Infantry, 160 men augmented by remnants of the 6th Infantry and the Missouri volunteers. This time the troops were able to drive the Seminoles from the hammock and towards the lake. Taylor then attacked their flank with his reserves, but the Seminoles were able to escape across the lake. Only about a dozen Seminoles had been killed in the battle. Nevertheless, the [Battle of Lake Okeechobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Okeechobee "Battle of Lake Okeechobee") was hailed as a great victory for Taylor and the Army.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-70)

## The Battle of Loxahatchee

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: The Battle of Loxahatchee")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_039.JPG/250px-Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_039.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_039.JPG)

Site of Battle of the Loxahatchee River plaque on wooden stump overlooking [Loxahatchee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loxahatchee_River "Loxahatchee River") in [Jonathan Dickinson State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park "Jonathan Dickinson State Park"). The actual battle is now known to have occurred about 4–5 miles (6.4–8.0 km) to the SW this marker.

Taylor now joined the other columns sweeping down the peninsula to pass on the east side of Lake Okeechobee, under the overall command of General Jesup. The troops along the Caloosahatchee River blocked any passage north on the west side of the lake. Still patrolling the east coast of Florida was the combined Army-Navy force under Navy Lt. Levin Powell. On January 15, Powell, in the [Battle of Jupiter Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jupiter_Inlet "Battle of Jupiter Inlet"), led eighty men towards a Seminole camp only to find themselves outnumbered by the Seminoles. A charge against the Seminoles was unsuccessful, but the troops made it back to their boats after losing four dead and twenty-two wounded. The party's retreat was covered by Army Lt. [Joseph E. Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._Johnston "Joseph E. Johnston"). At the end of January, Jesup's troops caught up with a large body of Seminoles to the east of Lake Okeechobee. The Seminoles were originally positioned in a hammock, but cannon and rocket fire drove them back across a wide stream (the [Loxahatchee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loxahatchee_River "Loxahatchee River")), where they made another stand. The Seminoles eventually just faded away, having caused more casualties than they received, and the Battle of Loxahatchee was over.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-71)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_036.JPG/250px-Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_036.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park_036.JPG)

Detail of plaque

The fighting now died down. In February 1838, Seminole chiefs Tuskegee and Halleck Hadjo approached Jesup with the proposition that they would stop fighting if they were allowed to stay south of Lake Okeechobee. Jesup favored the idea, foreseeing a long struggle to capture the remaining Seminoles in the [Everglades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everglades "Everglades"), and calculating that the Seminoles would be easier to round up later when the land was actually needed by white settlers. However, Jesup had to write to Washington for approval. The chiefs and their followers camped near the Army while awaiting the reply, and there was considerable fraternizing between the two camps. Secretary of War [Joel Roberts Poinsett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Roberts_Poinsett "Joel Roberts Poinsett") rejected the arrangement, however, and instructed Jesup to continue his campaign. Upon receiving Poinsett's response, Jesup summoned the chiefs to his camp, but they refused his invitation. Unwilling to let 500 Seminoles return to the swamps, Jesup sent a force to detain them. The Seminoles offered very little resistance, perhaps seeing little reason to continue fighting.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-72)

[Loxahatchee River Battlefield Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loxahatchee_River_Battlefield_Park "Loxahatchee River Battlefield Park") preserves an area of the fighting. Memorials are also located in [Jonathan Dickinson State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Dickinson_State_Park "Jonathan Dickinson State Park").

## Jesup steps down; Zachary Taylor takes command

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Jesup steps down; Zachary Taylor takes command")]

Jesup asked to be relieved of his command. As summer approached in 1838 the number of troops in Florida dwindled to about 2,300. In April, Jesup was informed that he should return to his position as Quartermaster General of the Army. In May, Zachary Taylor, now a General, assumed command of the Army forces in Florida. With reduced forces in Florida, Taylor concentrated on keeping the Seminole out of northern Florida, so that settlers could return to their homes. The Seminoles were still capable of reaching far north. In July they were thought responsible for the deaths of a family on the [Santa Fe River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe_River_(Florida) "Santa Fe River (Florida)"), another near Tallahassee, as well as two families in Georgia. The fighting died down during the summer, as the soldiers were pulled back to the coasts. The Seminoles concentrated on growing their crops and gathering supplies for fall and winter.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-73)

Taylor's plan was to build small posts at frequent intervals across northern Florida, connected by wagon roads, and to use larger units to search designated areas. This was expensive, but Congress continued to appropriate the necessary funds. In October 1838, Taylor relocated the last of the Seminole living along the Apalachicola River to Indian Territory west of the Mississippi River. Killings in the Tallahassee area caused Taylor to pull troops out of southern Florida to provide more protection in the north. The winter season was fairly quiet. The Army killed only a few Seminole and transported fewer than 200 to the West. Nine U.S. troops were killed by the Seminoles. Taylor reported in the Spring of 1839 that his men had constructed 53 new posts and cut 848 miles (1,365 km) of wagon roads.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-74)

## Macomb's peace and the Battle of Caloosahatchee

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Macomb's peace and the Battle of Caloosahatchee")]

In Washington and around the country in 1839, support for the war was eroding. The size of the Army had been increased because of the demands for manpower in the Florida war. Many people were beginning to think that the Seminole had earned a right to stay in Florida. The cost and time required to get all the Seminole out of Florida were looming larger. Congress appropriated US$5,000 to negotiate a settlement with the Seminole people in order to end the outlay of resources. President Martin Van Buren sent the Commanding General of the Army, [Alexander Macomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Macomb_(general) "Alexander Macomb (general)"), to negotiate a new treaty with the Seminole. Remembering the broken treaties and promises of the past, they were slow to respond to the new overtures. Finally, [Abiaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiaka "Abiaka") (Sam Jones) sent his chosen successor, Chitto Tustenuggee, to meet with Macomb. On May 19, 1839, Macomb announced reaching agreement with the Seminole. They would stop fighting in exchange for a reservation in southern Florida.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-75)

As the summer passed, the agreement seemed to be holding. There were few killings. A trading post was established on the north shore of the Caloosahatchee River, near present-day [Cape Coral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Coral,_Florida "Cape Coral, Florida"), and the Seminoles who came to the trading post seemed to be friendly. A detachment of 23 soldiers was stationed at the Caloosahatchee trading post under the command of Colonel [William S. Harney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Harney "William S. Harney"). On July 23, 1839, some 150 Indians, including [Holato Micco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Bowlegs "Billy Bowlegs") (Billy Bolek or Bowlegs) and two other leaders named [Chakaika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakaika "Chakaika") and Hospertarke, attacked the trading post and guard.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-76)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-77) Some of the soldiers, including Colonel Harney, were able to reach the river and find boats to escape in, but most of the soldiers, as well as a number of civilians in the trading post, were killed. The war was on again.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-78)

The Americans did not know which band of Indians had attacked the trading post. Many blamed the 'Spanish' Indians, led by Chakaika. Some suspected [Abiaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiaka "Abiaka") (Sam Jones), whose band of [Mikasuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikasuki "Mikasuki") had come to agreement with Macomb. Jones promised to turn the men responsible for the attack over to Harney in 33 days. In the meantime, the Mikasuki in Sam Jones' camp near [Fort Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida "Fort Lauderdale, Florida") remained on friendly terms with the local soldiers. On July 27 they invited the officers at the fort to a dance at the Mikasuki camp. The officers declined but sent two soldiers and a [Black Seminole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Seminoles "Black Seminoles") interpreter with a keg of whiskey. The Mikasuki killed the soldiers, but the Black Seminole escaped. He reported at the fort that Abiaka and [Chitto Tustenuggee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitto_Tustenuggee?action=edit&redlink=1 "Chitto Tustenuggee (page does not exist)") were involved in the attack. In August 1839, Seminole raiding parties operated as far north as [Fort White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_White,_Florida "Fort White, Florida").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-79)

## New tactics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: New tactics")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4d/Hunt900.jpg/250px-Hunt900.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hunt900.jpg)

This lithograph, published in 1848 after the war ended, depicts the common misperception that the bloodhounds physically attacked the Seminole.

The Army decided to use [bloodhounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodhound "Bloodhound") to track the Seminoles. (General Taylor had requested and received permission to buy bloodhounds in 1838) "Taylor accepted two of them for trial...the hounds failed their tests. They were trained to track [Negros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negros "Negros")...and could not be induced to nose out Indians."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-81) In early 1840, the Florida territorial government purchased [bloodhounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogo_cubano "Dogo cubano") from Cuba and hired Cuban handlers. Initial trials of the hounds had mixed results, and a public outcry arose against the use of the dogs, based on fears that they would be set on the Seminoles in physical attacks, including against women and children. The Secretary of War ordered the dogs to be muzzled and kept on leashes while tracking. Bloodhounds could not track through water, however "tracks of Indians were found, but the dogs finding the scent far different from that of a negro, refused to follow [them]."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-82)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-83)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-84)

In the north of Florida, Taylor's blockhouse and patrol system kept the Seminole on the move, but the Army could not clear them from the area. Ambushes of travelers were common. On February 13, 1840, the mail stage between St. Augustine and Jacksonville was ambushed. In May Seminole attacked a theatrical troupe near St. Augustine, killing a total of six people. In the same month, a group of four soldiers traveling between forts in Alachua County was attacked, with one killed and two others never seen again. A party of eighteen men pursued the Indians, but six were killed.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-85)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Seminole_War_in_Everglades.jpg/250px-Seminole_War_in_Everglades.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seminole_War_in_Everglades.jpg)

A [U.S. Marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") boat expedition searching for the Seminoles in the [Everglades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everglades "Everglades") during the Second Seminole War

In May 1840, Zachary Taylor, having served longer than any preceding commander in the Florida war, was granted his request for a transfer. He was replaced by Brig. Gen. [Walker Keith Armistead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_Keith_Armistead "Walker Keith Armistead"), who had earlier served in Florida as second in command to General Jesup. Armistead began an offensive, sending out 100 soldiers at a time to search for the Seminole and their camps. For the first time, the Army campaigned in Florida during the summer, taking captives and destroying crops and buildings. The Seminole also were active in warfare, killing fourteen soldiers during July.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-86) The Army worked to find the Seminole camps, burn their fields and stores of food, and drive off their livestock, including their horses.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-87)

Armistead planned to turn over the defense of Florida north of Fort King to the militia and volunteers. He wanted to use Army regulars to confine the Seminole to south of Fort King, and pursue them within that territory. The Army destroyed camps and fields across central Florida, a total of 500 acres (2.0 km 2) of Seminole crops by the middle of the summer. General Armistead became estranged from the territorial government, although he needed 1,500 militiamen from the Territory to defend the area north of Fort King. To bolster the effort south of Fort King, the Army sent the [Eighth Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "8th Infantry Regiment (United States)") to Florida. The Army in Florida now included ten companies of the Second Dragoon, nine companies of the Third Artillery, and the [First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "1st Infantry Regiment (United States)"), Second, [Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_United_States_Infantry_Regiment "3rd United States Infantry Regiment"), [Sixth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "6th Infantry Regiment (United States)"), Seventh and Eighth Infantry Regiments.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-88)

Changes were also being made in southern Florida. At Fort Bankhead on [Key Biscayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_Biscayne "Key Biscayne"), Col. Harney instituted an intensive training program in swamp and jungle warfare for his men.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlank199644%E2%80%9349-89) The Navy took a larger role in the war, sending manned boats with sailors and marines up rivers and streams, and into the Everglades.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-90)

## The "Mosquito Fleet"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: The \"Mosquito Fleet\"")]

In the early years of the war, Navy Lt. Levin Powell had commanded a joint Army-Navy force along with 8 Revenue Cutters of some 200 plus men that operated along the coast. In late 1839, Navy Lt. John T. McLaughlin was given command of a joint Army-Navy force supported by the [Revenue Marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Coast_Guard#The_Revenue_Marine "History of the United States Coast Guard"). This included [schooners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner") and [cutters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_(boat) "Cutter (boat)") off the shores, [barges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barge "Barge") close to the mainland to intercept Cuban and Bahamian traders bringing arms and other supplies to the Seminoles, and smaller boats, down to canoes, for patrolling up rivers and into the Everglades. McLaughlin established his base at [Tea Table Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Table_Key "Tea Table Key") in the upper [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-91)

An attempt to cross the Everglades from west to east was launched in April 1840, but the sailors and marines were engaged by Seminoles at the rendezvous point on [Cape Sable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Sable "Cape Sable"). Although there were no known fatalities (the Seminoles carried off their dead and wounded), many of the naval personnel became ill, and the expedition was called off and the sick were taken to Pensacola. For the next few months the men of Lt. McLaughlin's force explored the inlets and rivers of southern Florida.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-92) McLaughlin did lead a force across the Everglades later. Traveling from December 1840 to the middle of January 1841, McLaughlin's force crossed the Everglades from east to west in dugout canoes, the first groups of whites to complete a crossing.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-93)

## Indian Key

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Indian Key")]

[Indian Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Key_State_Historic_Site "Indian Key State Historic Site") is a small island in the upper [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys") which had developed into a base for [wreckers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrecking_(shipwreck) "Wrecking (shipwreck)"). In 1836 it became the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of the newly created [Dade County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County,_Florida "Miami-Dade County, Florida") and a [port of entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_entry "Port of entry"). Despite fears of attack and sightings of Indians in the area, the inhabitants of Indian Key stayed to protect their property, and to be close to any wrecks in the upper Keys. The islanders had six cannons and their own small militia company for their defense, and the Navy had established a base on nearby [Tea Table Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Table_Key "Tea Table Key").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViele199633%E2%80%9335-94)

Early in the morning of August 7, 1840, a large party of [Spanish Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Indians "Spanish Indians") snuck onto Indian Key. By chance, one man was up and raised the alarm after spotting the Indians. Of about fifty people living on the island, forty were able to escape. The dead included Dr. [Henry Perrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Perrine "Henry Perrine"), former United States [Consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consul_(representative) "Consul (representative)") in [Campeche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campeche,_Campeche "Campeche, Campeche"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), who was waiting at Indian Key until it was safe to take up a 36 sq mi (93 km 2) grant on the mainland that Congress had awarded to him.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEViele199635-95)

The naval base on Tea Table Key had been stripped of personnel for an operation on the southwest coast of the mainland, leaving only a physician, his patients, and five sailors under a midshipman to look after them. This small contingent mounted a couple of cannons on barges and tried to attack the Indians on Indian Key. The Indians fired back at the sailors with musket balls loaded in one of the cannons on shore. The recoil of the cannons on the barges broke them loose, sending them into the water, and the sailors had to retreat. The Indians burned the buildings on Indian Key after thoroughly looting it.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War#cite_note-96)

## Revenge and negotiations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_Seminole_War&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Revenge and negotiations")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/The_American_Soldier%2C_1839.jpg/250px-The_American_Soldier%2C_1839.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_American_Soldier,_1839.jpg)

A 20th century [McBarron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._Charles_McBarron_Jr. "H. Charles McBarron Jr.") illustration of U.S. Army troops with a Seminole guide.

In December 1840, Colonel [William S. Harney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Harney "William S. Harney") led ninety men into the Everglades from [Fort Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Dallas "Fort Dallas") on the [Miami River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_River_(Florida) "Miami River (Florida)"), traveling in canoes borrowed from the Marines. They were guided by a black man named John who had been in Seminole captivity for some time. The column encountered some Indians in canoes and gave chase, catching some of them and promptly hanging the men. When John was having trouble finding the way, Harney tried to force the captured Seminole women to lead the way to the camp, reportedly by threatening to hang their children.
